newsitem.title: UK: London metals market dismisses Hamanaka complaint.
newsitem.headline: London metals market dismisses Hamanaka complaint.

text.p: London market players dismissed remarks by disgraced copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka blaming the London Metal Exchange (LME) for some of his huge losses.
The former Sumitomo Corp trader said during his trial on Tuesday in Tokyo that "unfair intervention" by the LME forced him to unwind huge copper positions and incur losses.
"Mr Hamanaka is thrashing around looking for someone to blame and of course the LME is a rather obvious target," analyst Angus MacMillan of broker Billiton said.
"He is complaining because the LME didn't allow him to continue behaving in an irresponsible manner...it's ridiculous," he added.
Hamanaka, fired by Sumitomo in June 1996 and accused of losing $2.6 billion from unauthorised trades, has pleaded guilty to fraud and forgery charges. The trial is to determine his sentence.
Hamanaka said limits imposed by the LME in 1991 and 1993 on the backwardation, or the premium of cash metal over the nearby futures price, sparked some of his losses.
LME management were not immediately available to respond.
But floor traders on the LME were unimpressed by Hamanaka's comments. "What do you expect. He's just throwing the dirt," one said.
Hamanaka also complained that the LME, which has said it acted to maintain an orderly market, was not consistent in intervening in the market.
Others have also cried foul when the LME has slapped limits on the market, but the complaints are not usually valid, analysts and users of the LME said.
"We understand fully the LME's point of view," said Simon Payton, secretary general of the International Wrought Copper Council, which represents copper fabricators world-wide.
"Intervention is always a last resort. The power of intervention is not used lightly by the LME and it's always based on information that is known only to the LME and the LME executive."
If the LME set out hard and fast rules on when it would intervene, it would encourage unnecessary speculation, Payton said.
"If you could foresee what action the LME was going to take then you would be able to effectively speculate against what the LME would do," he said.

"One of the reasons why the tin agreement collapsed is because people knew what the (International) Tin Council (ITC) was going to do," Payton added, referring to the collapse of the ITC's buffer stock operations in 1985 and a plunge in tin prices.
Those who complain when the LME has intervened have usually over-extended themselves, analysts said.

"Intervention is by no means perfect, but usually you'll find the people who are complaining are people who have got themselves in a position due to every fault of their own and they complain when they have to pay the price for it," MacMillan said.
